lead.headline: Anthropic Sets $70-$78 IPO Range for a Nasdaq Debut Around Nov. 19 as Hot Inflation Puts a December Fed Hike at About 90%, Brent Jumps to $96 and Bitcoin Sinks Toward $69,000
lead.deck: Nvidia closed down 4.3% after its CEO's exit, gold fell about 3% on a 19-month-high dollar, and California gas is down to about $5.63 with oil now turning back up.

board_note: Figures as of Nov. 12-13 unless noted (mortgage and gas Nov. 5; this week's Freddie Mac survey not in sources read); sources in each story.

stories.headline: Anthropic Sets a $70-$78 IPO Range, Valuing It at Up to $1.404 Trillion, With Nasdaq Trading Expected Around Nov. 19 and Reported Demand Several Times the Shares on Offer
stories.deck: The range is well below the $2 trillion some outlets floated weeks ago, and up to 20% of the offering is expected to go to retail investors.
stories.summary: 825M shares at $70-$78 raise up to ~$64.4B; ticker ANT; Nasdaq ~Nov. 19; up to 20% retail.
paras: Disclosure: this briefing was written by Claude, an AI made by Anthropic. The facts below come from outside reporting. Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 a share for 825 million Class A shares, with underwriters holding an option on up to 123.75 million more. At the top of the range the offering raises about $64.4 billion and values the company at roughly $1.404 trillion on a fully diluted basis, up from $965 billion in a May funding round. The stock is to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, with trading expected around Nov. 19.

Alongside the public sale, seven strategic partners (AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC) agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price. Reporting says up to 20% of the public offering is expected to go to retail investors. One report, citing people familiar, put demand at about six times the shares on offer, though it cautioned that details could change.

The timing is awkward. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% last week on fears of tougher AI regulation after the midterms, and the company's annualized revenue run rate was reported at about $81 billion at the end of October, up from about $71 billion in late September. Pricing was expected during the week of Nov. 16, with the final range and date still subject to change.
money: Retail access does not mean a guaranteed allocation; brokerages usually ration IPO shares, and buying on the first day can mean paying well above the offer price.
If you own a Nasdaq-100 or total-market index fund, you may end up holding the stock indirectly once index providers add it, so check how much AI exposure you already have before buying more.
Newly listed mega-caps can swing 10% or more in days; sizing any purchase to an amount you could leave alone for years is a common way to limit regret.
Settled cash needs to be in your brokerage account before an IPO order, so decide ahead of time whether to move money out of savings or sell something else.

stories.when: Thu Nov 12 close | Earnings Tue Nov 17
stories.headline: Nvidia Closes Down 4.3% After an Early 14% Plunge on CEO Jensen Huang's Exit, While Downgrades Pile Up Before Tuesday's Earnings
stories.deck: Early reports of a roughly 10% drop overstated the closing damage, but analysts have slashed targets and the stock is down more than $1 trillion in value this month.
stories.summary: Huang out; Kress interim CEO; stock recovered half its loss to close -4.3%; Truist and Craig-Hallum cut to Hold; earnings Tuesday.
paras: Nvidia shares fell as much as 14% at Thursday's open after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, then recovered about half of that and closed down 4.3%. Yesterday's edition described a slide of about 10%; the final close was milder. The stock had already fallen about 27% from its record high through Wednesday, and one report put November losses above $1 trillion in market value.

CFO Colette Kress, who joined in 2013, is interim CEO while keeping her CFO role, and Harvey Jones, the company's first board chair, said the board has full confidence in her. One account tied the resignation to reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a subordinate, following a board investigation announced Sunday into reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

Analysts moved fast. Truist cut to Hold with a $174 target (from $346), Craig-Hallum cut to Hold with $180 (from $275), RBC cut its target to $230 from $330, and DA Davidson stayed at Buy but trimmed to $200 from $300. Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday, with a call at 2 p.m. PT, and management had earlier guided to about $108 billion in revenue.
money: Nvidia is now more than 6% of the S&P 500, so even index-fund owners feel its swings; check how concentrated your 401(k) or IRA is in a handful of mega-cap tech names.
Earnings on Tuesday could move the stock sharply either way; many investors avoid making big single-stock bets right before a known event.
If you are tempted to buy the dip, spreading purchases over several weeks reduces the risk of picking the wrong day.
If you hold Nvidia at a loss in a taxable account, selling to harvest the loss can offset gains, but the wash-sale rule blocks repurchase within 30 days.

stories.when: Fed meets Dec 8-9 | PPI Fri Nov 13
stories.headline: A December Fed Rate Hike Is Now Priced at About 90% After Hot October Inflation, With the 10-Year Treasury Yield Back Above 5%
stories.deck: Futures even give a half-point move an 11% chance, up from zero before the CPI report; the dollar hit a 19-month high.
stories.summary: CPI +0.35% m/m, core +0.30%; 10-yr at 5.12% Thursday; CME shows ~89% odds of a quarter-point hike.
paras: October consumer prices rose about 0.35% from September, with core prices up 0.30%, according to Wolf Street's analysis of the report. Because the government did not collect October 2025 price data during the shutdown, year-over-year rates are estimates: roughly 4.0% for headline and 2.8% for core. Services did the damage: non-housing services rose 0.45% in the month, led by airfares, recreation and auto insurance.

Bond yields jumped. The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 12 basis points to roughly 5.0% on CPI day, a $42 billion 10-year auction cleared at 5.02%, and the yield reached 5.12% on Thursday from 4.98% on Tuesday. According to CME's FedWatch tool as cited by one precious-metals report, traders see about an 89% chance of a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting and an 11% chance of a half-point hike.
The next test is the producer price index due Friday. A cooler reading could ease pressure on the dollar and yields, while another hot one would reinforce the hike case.
money: Variable-rate debt such as credit cards and home-equity lines tends to reprice quickly after Fed hikes, so paying down the highest-rate balance first is the most direct response.
High-yield savings and money-market rates usually rise with Fed hikes; it can be worth checking whether your bank passes increases along.
Longer-dated Treasuries now yield above 5%, which some savers use for money they will not need for several years, though prices fall if yields keep rising.
Mortgage shoppers watch the 10-year yield more than the Fed itself; locking a rate when the yield dips can matter.

stories.headline: Stocks Slip About 0.4% Thursday After a Wild Open, With the S&P 500 at 7,592.40 as Nvidia Swings and Oil Jumps
stories.deck: The Dow closed at 52,297.09 and the Nasdaq at 25,366.09; jobless claims stayed low at 189,000.
stories.summary: S&P 500 -26.98 to 7,592.40; Dow -189.40; Nasdaq -100.10; Broadcom and AMD rose while CoreWeave fell.
paras: Wall Street recovered most of its early losses but still finished lower Thursday. The S&P 500 fell 26.98 points to 7,592.40, the Dow lost 189.40 to 52,297.09 and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 100.10 to 25,366.09, each about 0.4%. The S&P had been down nearly 1% at the open before swinging positive in the morning.

Chip stocks split. Broadcom rose 5.5% and AMD 5.9%, while CoreWeave fell 6.9% and Micron slipped 1.6%. Energy shares gained with oil: ExxonMobil rose 1.8% and Marathon Petroleum 2.5%. For comparison, the S&P 500 had jumped 2.4% on Monday to 7,549.94 on falling oil prices and anticipation of inflation data.

On the economy, weekly jobless claims were 189,000, which remains low by historical standards, and existing-home sales were due out the same day. Cisco and Applied Materials were among the companies scheduled to report.
money: A day like this shows how much swinging underneath a flat index; if you rebalance, doing it on a schedule beats reacting to daily moves.
Low jobless claims mean layoffs are not yet spreading, which is why the Fed can focus on inflation; keep an eye on claims as a gauge of job security.
Energy shares rose while tech sagged; owning a broad index fund already spreads that risk across sectors.
Long-term investors often keep cash for the next six to twelve months of expenses outside the market so a drop never forces a sale.

stories.headline: Bitcoin Drops to About $68,850, a Near Three-Month Low, as Fed Hike Bets, ETF Outflows and an MSCI Decision on Strategy Weigh
stories.deck: The coin was near $73,660 on Thursday, then fell more than 6% in 24 hours as stablecoin supply shrank at the fastest pace since 2022.
stories.summary: BTC ~$68.9K early Friday (-6.6% in 24h); spot ETFs lost $1.44B in five sessions; MSCI dropping Strategy.
paras: Bitcoin slid to about $68,850 in early trading Friday, a near three-month low, down about 6.6% over 24 hours and 9% for the week. On Thursday it had traded near $73,660 after bouncing from a $72,787 low following the hot inflation report, and it remains well below its roughly $87,600 level at the start of the year.

Several pressures hit at once. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.44 billion of net outflows over the five sessions through Nov. 11. Expectations of a December Fed hike weigh on assets that pay no yield. MSCI plans to remove Strategy, Metaplanet and Yellow Cake from its global indexes, and Strategy had warned that an exclusion could force about $2.8 billion of stock sales. Stablecoin supply also shrank by $14.2 billion over 30 days, the sharpest drop since 2022.

Analysts called the near-term outlook bearish and are watching whether $70,000 holds. Some traders also link the weakness to Democrats' midterm gains and the possibility of more congressional attention to crypto. Ether was near $2,049 on Thursday.
money: Crypto trades around the clock, so losses can pile up while you sleep; many holders cap crypto at a small share of their total investments.
Selling at a loss in a taxable account can create a capital loss that offsets gains, and crypto wash-sale treatment has differed from stocks, so check current IRS guidance before relying on it.
Crypto-linked stocks and ETFs carry extra risk from index changes like MSCI's; check what your funds actually hold.
Spreading purchases over time, rather than one lump sum, is a common way to avoid buying a local top.

stories.headline: Gold Falls About 3% to Roughly $3,866 and Silver Slips Back Under $50 as the Dollar Hits a 19-Month High
stories.deck: The slide, not new gold news, is blamed on rising yields and Fed hike bets; gold is near its late-October one-year low.
stories.summary: Gold ~$3,866.51 (-3.05%), silver ~$49.88 (-3.5%); December futures opened under $4,000 for the first time since last week.
paras: Gold dropped about 3.05% Thursday to roughly $3,866.51 an ounce, its third straight daily decline, while silver fell about 3.5% to $49.88 and platinum eased about 1.4% to $1,517.70. December futures had opened at $3,994, back under $4,000 for the first time since last week, and gold is now close to its late-October one-year low near $3,870.

The cause is the dollar, which rallied to a 19-month high as hotter inflation lifted Treasury yields and Fed hike expectations. Higher yields make non-interest-paying gold less attractive. Analyst Ole Hansen pointed to support near $3,970 and noted that lower energy prices could eventually ease inflation, which would weaken the hike case.

One report calls the area a possible accumulation zone for physical buyers rather than a trend change, but that is opinion, not a forecast. Friday's producer price index is the next signal for the dollar.
money: Gold has fallen roughly 5% in a month; if you hold it as insurance, the price drop is a reminder it is volatile too.
Buying coins or bars carries dealer premiums over spot and resale spreads, which eat into short-term gains.
A stronger dollar makes imports and foreign travel cheaper for Angelenos; it is an input to planning overseas trips.
Gold ETFs avoid storage costs but still move with the same price; a small share of a portfolio is a common approach.

stories.headline: Brent Jumps 3.3% to $95.82 After Trump Says the U.S. Does Not Need an Iran Deal, Though Crude Has Been Far Below Its Wartime Peak
stories.deck: Oil has swung between roughly $70 and $150 since the war with Iran began in late February.
stories.summary: Brent +3.3% to $95.82 Thursday; WTI and Brent had been falling earlier in the week; energy stocks led.
paras: Brent crude settled up 3.3% at $95.82 a barrel Thursday, after briefly jumping from about $92 to above $94 in the morning when President Trump posted that the U.S. does not need a deal with Iran. Earlier in the week crude had been sliding: on Monday WTI fell to $85.93 and Brent to $91.75 as investors awaited the inflation report.

Since the U.S.-Israel war with Iran began in late February, oil has traded between roughly $70 and $150 a barrel, so Thursday's move is small against that range but reverses the hopes for a settlement that had pushed prices lower. Energy shares rallied, with ExxonMobil up 1.8% and Marathon Petroleum up 2.5%.
The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.12% in the same session, keeping the oil-inflation-rates loop in focus for the Fed.
money: Oil feeds into gasoline and airfares within weeks; locking in holiday flights sooner can beat waiting if oil keeps rising.
California gas has been falling, and a jump in crude can stop that trend; fill up when stations are cheap rather than on a fixed schedule.
Energy stocks gained on the news; broad index funds already hold energy, so you may not need separate bets.
If you run a delivery or rideshare business, tracking fuel costs weekly helps with pricing and tax deductions.

stories.when: NAR released Nov 12 | Freddie Mac Nov 5
stories.headline: Existing-Home Sales Fell 5.5% in October to the Slowest Pace in More Than 16 Years Reports Say, While Mortgage Rates Were 7.18% at Last Reading
stories.deck: With the 10-year Treasury yield back above 5%, the recent run of falling mortgage rates may not continue.
stories.summary: October existing-home sales -5.5% m/m (Sept: 3.99M), down year over year in all four regions; 30-yr rate 7.18% on Nov. 5.
paras: The National Association of Realtors reported Thursday that existing-home sales fell 5.5% in October from September, when sales ran at 3.99 million, and were down from a year earlier in all four regions. A market report described it as the slowest pace in more than 16 years.

Freddie Mac's most recent survey in the sources read, from Nov. 5, put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 7.18%, down from 7.24% the week before, with the 15-year at 6.57%. That was the third straight weekly decline, but the 10-year Treasury yield has since climbed to 5.12%, which usually pushes mortgage rates up. This week's survey was not in sources read.
The combination of high rates and weak sales leaves many would-be buyers and sellers waiting, which also helps explain softer rents in parts of Los Angeles.
money: At 7.18%, each $100,000 borrowed costs roughly $680 a month in principal and interest; shopping three or more lenders often shaves a fraction of a point.
Sellers who bought with low rates are reluctant to move, which keeps inventory tight; buyers sometimes negotiate seller-paid rate buydowns instead of price cuts.
If you have a higher-rate loan, refinancing math only works if rates fall meaningfully; run the break-even on closing costs before acting.
Renters facing flat rents can use that as leverage when renewing.

stories.headline: Three IPOs Were Slated This Week, Led by a $214 Million Swiss Dental-Tech Deal, Ahead of Anthropic's Far Larger Offering
stories.deck: Renaissance Capital says the backdrop looks weaker than the company likely expected after the post-midterm tech sell-off.
stories.summary: vVardis $214M, Rezera $200M, Windward Bio $175M; Anthropic could launch as soon as this week.
paras: Disclosure: this briefing was written by Claude, an AI made by Anthropic. The facts below come from outside reporting. Renaissance Capital's weekly preview listed three IPOs for the week of Nov. 9: vVardis, a Swiss maker of non-invasive cavity treatments, seeking $214 million at $21-$24 a share; Rezera, a Boston developer of oral inflammation drugs, seeking $200 million at $11-$13; and Windward Bio, a Swiss respiratory biotech, seeking $175 million at $16-$18. The preview did not give exact listing dates.

The same preview said Anthropic could launch its IPO as early as Tuesday, with pricing possibly in the week of Nov. 16, and described the market as weaker than the company probably wanted after tech stocks fell sharply following the midterm results.
money: Small IPOs, especially biotech, can be volatile and illiquid; many investors treat them as a tiny speculative slice, if at all.
Retail investors often cannot get IPO allocations at the offer price, so first-day buyers frequently pay a premium.
Quiet periods and lockups matter: insiders usually cannot sell right away, and expirations can pressure prices later.
Reading the prospectus's risk factors takes minutes and often shows the real story.

stories.headline: The U.S.-China Trade Truce Now Runs to Jan. 10, 2027, but Bessent Calls It a Checkpoint and No New Tariff Cuts Came With It
stories.deck: Suspensions of new retaliatory tariffs, rare-earth export controls and port fees stay in place while talks on a bigger package continue.
stories.summary: Extended two months from Nov. 10; USTR proposed port-fee suspension through Jan. 9; China stack unchanged.
paras: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced on Sept. 23 that the Busan truce, due to expire Nov. 10, 2026, would run to Jan. 10, 2027. It keeps in place the U.S. suspension of new retaliatory tariffs on China, a mutual suspension of new rare-earth and high-tech export controls, and the Section 301 maritime action on port fees and certain duties. USTR proposed extending the maritime suspension through Jan. 9, though that was not final when the guide was published.

The extension did not cut tariffs. The current China stack, as described, is the regular duty plus a 12.5% Section 301 forced-labor tariff, product-specific Section 301 rates and Section 232 metals duties. Bessent said a broader economic package could be agreed by January, or the current arrangement could roll forward again; topics such as AI and chip export controls and Taiwan arms sales were reported as under discussion only.
If neither side acts before Jan. 10, suspended threats and export-control suspensions would be live again under whatever legal authorities apply.
money: Importers and small online sellers who source from China should price Q1 inventory with a possible January tariff reset in mind.
Consumers buying electronics or cranes-and-equipment-adjacent goods may see price changes if the truce lapses; early-winter sales can be a hedge.
Farm-export-linked and rare-earth-dependent companies swing on truce headlines; diversify rather than bet on a single outcome.
Watch the Dec. 4 polysilicon tariff for solar costs.

stories.headline: Tariffs by the Calendar: Polysilicon Dec. 4, Furniture and Cabinets Step Up Jan. 1, Nicaragua Jan. 1, Drone Components Feb. 9
stories.deck: The trade-compliance tracker shows a steady drumbeat of sector duties even as the courts review others.
stories.summary: Polysilicon 10%-15% Dec. 4; furniture to 30% and cabinets to 50% Jan. 1; drone parts 25% Feb. 9.
paras: Section 232 tariffs and minimum import prices on polysilicon take effect Dec. 4: 10% for the UK, 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan and Liechtenstein, and 15% for other countries. On Jan. 1, 2027, the 25% duty on upholstered wooden furniture and on kitchen cabinets and vanities for most countries is scheduled to rise to 30% for furniture and 50% for cabinets and vanities.

Also on Jan. 1, the Section 301 rate on Nicaraguan goods not originating under CAFTA-DR rises from 0% to 10%, then to 15% in 2028. A 25% tariff on certain unmanned-aircraft components takes effect Feb. 9, 2027, and status reports on robotics and industrial machinery (Apr. 26) and wind turbines (Apr. 20) are due in April.
money: Remodelers and homeowners planning a kitchen project may want to order cabinets before Jan. 1 if a quote is firm; ask suppliers whether prices already reflect the step-up.
Solar installers could see module costs rise after Dec. 4, which is relevant if you are comparing quotes this month.
Furniture is a common holiday purchase; sales may not offset tariff cost increases early next year.
Small businesses can ask customs brokers about duty drawback and classification before the dates.

stories.headline: Canada Faces 50% Section 338 Duties Since Aug. 22, With Scope Changes Sept. 15 and Oct. 30 and Ottawa's Counter-Tariffs on About $27.6 Billion of U.S. Goods
stories.deck: Retaliation took effect Sept. 8, meaning California exporters and cross-border shoppers feel it from both sides.
stories.summary: 50% U.S. duty on Canadian goods; scope adjusted twice; Canada hits back on ~$27.6B.
paras: According to the trade-compliance tracker, a 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian goods took effect Aug. 22, 2026, with scope changes effective Sept. 15 and Oct. 30. Canada's counter-tariffs on about $27.6 billion of U.S. products took effect Sept. 8.

Separately, Section 301 forced-labor tariffs of 10% to 12.5% depending on the country took effect July 24, with exemptions for Section 232 goods and USMCA-qualifying goods. Pending investigations on Germany and Ireland (excess capacity) and Vietnam (intellectual property) have rates still to be set.
money: Anyone importing Canadian lumber-adjacent or consumer goods should check the latest product list before ordering.
Canadian retaliation raises prices on some U.S. exports, which can hit California food and goods sellers; diversification of buyers helps.
USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt from the Section 301 forced-labor tariffs; confirming origin paperwork can save duty.
Travelers shopping across the border should check updated personal-exemption and duty rules.

stories.headline: A Trade Court Declared the Section 122 Tariff Proclamation Invalid in May, but With No Universal Injunction Customs Is Still Collecting While the Government Appeals
stories.deck: The ruling shows how tariff authority is still being fought in court even as new tariffs rest on other laws.
stories.summary: CIT ruled Proclamation 11012 invalid May 7; no universal injunction; collection continues pending appeal.
paras: The Court of International Trade declared Proclamation 11012, the Section 122 tariff action, invalid on May 7, 2026, but did not issue a universal injunction, so Customs and Border Protection continues to collect the duties. The government has appealed, and the tracker does not report later developments.

The Supreme Court earlier struck down the IEEPA tariffs, which is why the Busan fentanyl-tariff reduction no longer affects the China rate; newer tariffs now rest on Sections 232, 301 and 338 instead.
money: Importers may want to document duties paid under challenged authorities in case refunds become available later.
Consumers are unlikely to see refunds directly; the money flows to importers of record.
Because legal outcomes can take months, businesses often budget as if duties will stick.
Trade-law news can move retail and shipping stocks; avoid trading on the first headline.

stories.headline: Tariff Refunds Via CBP's CAPE Process Are Generally Due Within 60-90 Days of Acceptance, but Some Entries Remain Ineligible and the Government Is Appealing on Finally Liquidated Ones
stories.deck: Entries on drawback claims or under open protest are not yet eligible.
stories.summary: CAPE launched Apr. 20; refunds ~60-90 days after acceptance; appeal covers finally liquidated entries.
paras: Customs and Border Protection launched its CAPE refund functionality for IEEPA duties on Apr. 20, 2026, and expects refunds generally within 60 to 90 days of acceptance. Entries on drawback claims, under open protest or otherwise excluded are not yet eligible.

The government is appealing the part of the Court of International Trade order covering finally liquidated entries, so importers whose entries were already finalized may not get money until that is resolved. The refunds go to importers of record, not to consumers who paid higher prices.
money: Small importers should confirm whether their entries are open or finally liquidated; deadlines for protests are short.
Customs brokers often handle CAPE filings; compare fees against the refund size.
Consumers will not get direct refunds, but retailers receiving refunds may help prices stabilize over time.
Keep import records for years; refund programs often reward good documentation.

stories.headline: Trump Says the U.S. Does Not Need a Deal With Iran, Sidelining Vance's Outreach, and Rubio Says Washington Is in No Hurry as Both Sides Run Competing Blockades
stories.deck: The reversal came days after talk of momentum toward a settlement; oil jumped, but the war has already pushed it between $70 and $150.
stories.summary: Trump posts there is no need for a deal; Vance's planned contact reportedly sidelined; Brent +3.3%.
paras: President Trump said Thursday that the U.S. no longer wants negotiations with Iran, writing that the U.S. does not need a deal. The statement reversed comments earlier in the week about momentum toward a settlement and sidelined Vice President JD Vance, who had been trying to arrange a meeting with a senior Iranian official in Qatar; Iran denied any talks were scheduled.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. was in no hurry because it believed it held the upper hand in the Strait of Hormuz, where both sides are running competing blockades. Regional partners warned of prolonged uncertainty. Brent briefly jumped above $94 on the post and finished the day up 3.3% at $95.82.
money: Fuel is the main household link; California gas has fallen for six straight weeks, but renewed war risk can reverse that quickly.
Airlines and shippers pass on fuel costs with a lag; book travel earlier if prices are rising.
Defense and energy stocks often rise on escalation, but index funds already hold both.
Keeping a small cash buffer for volatile energy bills is a conventional hedge.

stories.when: Talks ended Nov 11 | Envoys in Moscow Thu
stories.headline: Abu Dhabi Talks End With a Large Prisoner Swap but No Peace Breakthrough as Kushner and Witkoff Brief Putin in Moscow, Then Meet Zelensky in Ireland
stories.deck: Territory, Europe's seat at the table and mutual distrust remain the sticking points.
stories.summary: First trilateral meeting since the Iran war began; swap agreed; Russia rejects European role.
paras: The two-day, U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi ended Wednesday with an agreement on a major prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on peace. Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said understandings were reached in some places and not others, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the meeting very productive while saying a breakthrough will take time.

Sticking points include Moscow's territorial claims, which Ukraine rejects, Russia's rejection of a European role that Washington wants, and what Jared Kushner called deep distrust. Kushner and Steve Witkoff planned to brief Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday and then meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Ireland. One headline on a news page suggested Putin agreed to let Europe join, but the article body did not confirm it.
money: Peace headlines have repeatedly moved oil and European energy prices; changes in your fuel and utility costs are the likelier channel.
Defense and grain-related stocks react to talks news; avoid trading on the first report.
Sanctions relief or tightening can affect fertilizer and commodity prices over months.
Diversified funds absorb headline risk better than single-theme bets.

stories.headline: Shutdown Clock: Federal Funding Runs Out Dec. 11, Full-Year Bills Are Not Done and a Stopgap Looks Likelier as Congress Gets Back to Work
stories.deck: Appropriations chair Tom Cole reportedly said there is not enough time to finish the bills.
stories.summary: Stopgap CR (H.R. 6500) runs through Dec. 11; agencies would begin shutting at 12:01 a.m. Dec. 12 without action.
paras: The stopgap law the House passed 370-48 on Sept. 1 and Trump signed Sept. 2 funds the government through Friday, Dec. 11, 2026. If Congress passes neither full-year bills nor another stopgap by then, agencies without funding would begin shutting down at 12:01 a.m. on Saturday, Dec. 12. The Senate passed its version in July, 90-6.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole reportedly said there is not enough time to finish the full-year bills, raising the odds of another stopgap. Congress returned Nov. 9 for a lame-duck session described as far from a deal, with a tentative Senate Thanksgiving recess Nov. 23-27 and a second recess Dec. 21-31. In past shutdowns Social Security and SSI payments continued and the Postal Service kept delivering mail; the most recent full shutdown lasted 43 days, from Oct. 1 to Nov. 12, 2025.
money: Federal workers and contractors commonly build a cushion of a few weeks of expenses in December; check your credit union's shutdown loan programs.
Shutdowns delay some data releases and permits; plans that depend on federal approvals may slip.
Markets have usually reacted modestly to shutdowns; the bigger risk is panic selling.
SNAP and other programs can be affected by long lapses; know your county's backup resources.

stories.headline: Anthropic Commits $3.4 Billion for 1.7 Gigawatts of Gas Generators, the Largest Direct Power-Equipment Buy by an AI Company, as Its S-1 Flags Power as a Constraint
stories.deck: The deal takes over Caterpillar-linked generator commitments from OnePWR Solutions and should deliver within about two years.
stories.summary: $3.4B for 1.7 GW; supplier OnePWR; S-1 discloses ~$900.9B in committed compute and infrastructure spending.
paras: Disclosure: this briefing was written by Claude, an AI made by Anthropic. The facts below come from outside reporting. Anthropic is committing $3.4 billion to secure 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty natural gas generators for its data centers, which the Financial Times described as the largest direct investment in power-generation equipment by an AI company. The supplier is OnePWR Solutions of San Antonio, and Anthropic took over generator commitments OnePWR had made with Caterpillar. The generators are expected to become available within about two years.

The company's S-1 flags power as a major constraint, warning that electrical equipment can take years to procure and may cost above market rates, and that gas-dependent sites face fuel-price volatility and pipeline limits. It discloses about $900.9 billion in aggregate committed computing and infrastructure spending. Other AI firms are also securing power: Alphabet bought Intersect Power for $4.75 billion, xAI uses gas turbines, Meta is building on-site gas generation in Ohio, and Microsoft and Amazon have nuclear agreements.
money: AI's power appetite can push up regional electricity prices over time; compare your utility's rate plans and time-of-use options.
Gas-turbine and electrical-equipment makers are a way investors play the buildout, but those stocks already reflect much of it.
Home energy efficiency and solar-plus-storage can hedge against rising rates.
Check whether your utility is proposing data-center-related rate cases; public comment periods are open to ratepayers.

stories.headline: Seven Chip and Cloud Giants Will Buy $26 Billion of Anthropic Stock Alongside the IPO, While Revenue Run Rate Reached About $81 Billion
stories.deck: AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC would hold non-voting Class N shares bought at the IPO price.
stories.summary: $26B private placement to seven strategic partners; run rate ~$81B at end of October vs ~$71B in late September.
paras: Disclosure: this briefing was written by Claude, an AI made by Anthropic. The facts below come from outside reporting. Alongside the public offering, seven strategic partners agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price: AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. Combined with the public sale of up to $64.4 billion, reports say the sales would exceed SpaceX's June listing as a record.

Fortune reported the company's annualized revenue run rate reached about $81 billion at the end of October, up from roughly $71 billion in late September. The circular nature of the deals, with chip and cloud suppliers investing in a major customer, is part of what analysts debate when judging how durable AI spending is.
money: When your suppliers are also investors, revenue can look stronger than demand from independent customers; reading how analysts discuss it helps.
Index funds will eventually hold more of these linked companies, concentrating risk in a few names.
AI-linked stocks fell sharply last week; diversification beyond tech is the standard cushion.
Consider whether your employer's stock plus your funds already overweight AI.

stories.headline: AI Stocks Whipsaw After the Midterms: The Nasdaq Fell 5.5% Last Week on Regulation Fears, Then Rebounded Monday as the S&P 500 Jumped 2.4%
stories.deck: Chip leaders are split this week, with Broadcom and AMD rising on Thursday while CoreWeave fell.
stories.summary: Post-midterm AI sell-off erased nearly $2.5 trillion in one session; Monday rebound; Thursday mixed.
paras: Disclosure: this briefing was written by Claude, an AI made by Anthropic. The facts below come from outside reporting. Fortune reported that after Democrats' midterm gains, the AI sector sold off sharply on fears of stricter regulation and tougher scrutiny of data-center buildouts. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% last week, erasing nearly $2.5 trillion of market value in one session, and some analysts warned it was nearing correction territory.

Stocks rebounded Monday, with the S&P 500 up 2.4% to 7,549.94, and on Thursday chip leaders split: Broadcom rose 5.5% and AMD 5.9% while CoreWeave fell 6.9%. A market report said the swings suggest Wall Street sees limited fallout for the AI industry from Nvidia's CEO change.
money: If AI names dominate your 401(k), check whether target-date or index funds already overweight them.
Regulation risk cuts both ways: it can slow AI spending but also reduce risks of overbuilding.
Rebalancing after big swings brings your portfolio back to your plan.
Avoid margin on volatile tech positions; forced selling magnifies losses.

stories.headline: California Gas Averages $5.63 and Los Angeles-Long Beach $5.70, Down 20 Cents in a Week for a Sixth Straight Weekly Drop, but Thursday's Oil Jump Threatens the Trend
stories.deck: LA County hit its lowest level since Sept. 4 last week, and the national average fell for 13 straight days.
stories.summary: CA $5.63, LA-LB $5.70, U.S. $3.90 (as of Nov. 5); LA County $5.871 on Nov. 6.
paras: The Auto Club reported that, as of Nov. 5, Los Angeles-Long Beach regular averaged $5.70, California $5.63 and the nation $3.90, each about 20 cents lower than a week earlier and 83 to 94 cents above a year ago. It was the sixth straight weekly drop, which AAA attributed to oil under $100 and seasonal demand declines.

Another daily tally had the LA County average at $5.871 on Nov. 6, down 53.6 cents in a month and still $1.02 above a year ago, and the lowest since Sept. 4; the national average had fallen 13 straight days. The Auto Club said lower oil could keep prices falling, but Brent rose 3.3% Thursday to $95.82.
money: Prices vary by $1 or more across LA neighborhoods; checking a price app before filling up saves real money.
Warehouse-club and grocery fuel programs often undercut stations by 20 to 40 cents.
With prices still about a dollar above last year, a fuel-efficient driving routine matters more than waiting.
Holiday travelers should price flights now as fuel costs feed fares.

sources.t: Auto Club: gas prices continue downward rapidly for sixth straight week (AAA/Auto Club)
Average LA County gas price drops to lowest amount since Sept. 4 (MyNewsLA)

stories.headline: What October's Hot Inflation Hit: Airfares Up 0.84%, Auto Insurance Up 0.71% and Groceries Up 0.44% in a Month
stories.deck: Rent of primary residence rose just 0.20% in the month, about 2.9% year over year by one analyst's estimate.
stories.summary: Core services +0.34%; non-housing services +0.45%; food at home +0.44%; energy +0.70%.
paras: Wolf Street's analysis of the October report found non-housing services up 0.45% in the month, with recreation services up 0.82%, airfares and public transportation up 0.84% and auto insurance up 0.71%. Food at home rose 0.44%, energy rose 0.70% and core goods rose 0.39%.

Housing was calmer: rent of primary residence rose 0.20% and owners' equivalent rent 0.32%. Year-over-year figures are estimates because the government did not collect October 2025 pricing during the shutdown. The report pushed yields higher and revived Fed rate-hike bets.
money: Auto insurance is rising fast; shopping quotes at renewal and asking about discounts can save hundreds a year.
Grocery costs are climbing; store brands and bulk buys help blunt the increase.
Flat-ish rents give renters leverage at renewal, especially in Los Angeles where listings have been soft.
Wages that trail inflation make a monthly budget review more valuable.

stories.headline: 2027 Tax Numbers Are Set: Standard Deduction $16,600 Single, $33,200 Joint and $24,925 Head of Household, Child Credit $2,300, Gift Exclusion $20,000
stories.deck: The top 37% bracket starts above $661,375 for singles and $793,650 for joint filers; these apply to returns filed in 2028.
stories.summary: Standard deduction up $1,000 joint; CTC $2,300 ($1,800 refundable); health FSA $3,500; EITC max $8,496 (3+ kids).
paras: The IRS's 2027 inflation adjustments set the standard deduction at $33,200 for joint filers (up $1,000), $16,600 for single filers and $24,925 for heads of household. The child tax credit rises $100 to $2,300, with $1,800 refundable. The annual gift exclusion is $20,000, up from $19,000, and the estate exclusion is $15.48 million.

Other limits include a health FSA cap of $3,500 with a $700 carryover, a maximum earned income credit of $8,496 for families with three or more children, a $350 monthly transit and parking fringe and an adoption credit up to $18,250. One report notes some figures in the source article look garbled, so check the revenue procedure before relying on less common limits.
money: Higher deductions mean more income is shielded; adjust withholding via a new W-4 only if your situation changed.
A $3,500 health FSA cap lets you set aside more pre-tax for medical costs; plan during open enrollment.
Families with children should confirm credit eligibility, especially the refundable portion.
Gifts up to $20,000 per person can be made tax-free of gift-tax reporting.

sources.t: IRS adjusts tax brackets, standard deduction for tax year 2027 (CPA Practice Advisor)
IRS sets inflation adjustments for tax year 2027 (Accounting Today)

stories.headline: California FAIR Plan Rates Rise 29.1% on Average for More Than 675,000 Customers Since Oct. 15, and Some Wildfire-Zone Premiums Could Double
stories.deck: A Stanford study found California homeowners' premiums up 84% since 2020, and FAIR Plan share of homes rose from under 2% to 5%.
stories.summary: Average +29.1% at renewal on or after Oct. 15; some pay more than double; private insurers are writing again.
paras: The California FAIR Plan, the state's insurer of last resort, is raising rates by an average of 29.1% at renewals on or after Oct. 15, affecting more than 675,000 customers. The plan had asked for 35.8%. Increases vary by home: homes near high wildfire-risk areas could see much more, some wildfire premiums could double, while lower-risk and some urban Bay Area policyholders may pay less.

A June Stanford study found homeowners' premiums are up 84% since 2020 and FAIR Plan enrollment rose from under 2% to 5% of homes. KQED noted more traditional insurers are writing in California again, so some FAIR Plan customers may find private coverage, though mountain residents say finding any insurer is the harder problem.
money: Get quotes from at least three private insurers or a broker before your FAIR Plan renewal.
Mitigation steps such as defensible space and ember-resistant vents can lower premiums with some insurers.
FAIR Plan policies typically cover fire only, so a separate difference-in-conditions policy may be needed.
Keep a home inventory and photos in case of a claim.

stories.headline: New California Work Laws for 2027: Bereavement Leave for a 'Designated Person,' a Revised Stay-or-Pay Ban and a $19.75 Farmworker Minimum
stories.deck: Employers with five or more workers must allow bereavement leave, and repeat pay-data filing failures could cost up to $1,000 per employee.
stories.summary: SB 1149 bereavement; AB 1697 stay-or-pay ban Jan. 1, 2027; AB 2646 ag minimum $19.75; SB 1237 penalties.
paras: A law-firm roundup of what Gov. Newsom signed says that, unless noted, new laws take effect Jan. 1, 2027. SB 1149 requires employers with five or more employees to allow bereavement leave for the death of a designated person, which can include extended relatives or chosen family, with employers allowed to limit it to one designated person per 12 months. AB 2646 sets a $19.75 hourly minimum for approved agricultural employees, indexed annually.

AB 1697 delays the operative date of the stay-or-pay ban (AB 692) to Jan. 1, 2027, adding exemptions for certain grant-funded recruitment and retention bonuses, repayment of advanced PTO on voluntary separation and some securities and insurance affiliation agreements. SB 1237 raises the penalty for repeat failures to file the pay data report to up to $1,000 per employee, with the filing due in May 2027 for employers with 100 or more employees.
money: Check your offer letter or bonus agreement for repayment terms before signing; the stay-or-pay rules change what can be clawed back.
If you lose a loved one, ask HR about the designated-person leave starting in 2027.
Small employers should update handbooks now to avoid penalties.
Farmworkers should confirm which program rate applies to them.

sources.t: California's new employment laws for 2027 (California Employment Law Report)
State quick hits: California privacy and AI legislative updates (Venable)

stories.headline: Covered California Open Enrollment Runs to Jan. 31 With Expanded State Help for Incomes up to 200% of Poverty, and 55% of Enrollees See No Premium Increase
stories.deck: State subsidy funding rises to $300 million, but it cannot fully replace about $2.5 billion in lost federal aid.
stories.summary: Plan by Dec. 31 for Jan. 1 coverage; 358,000 pay $0; state aid up to $31,920 single or $66,000 for a family of four.
paras: Covered California's 2027 open enrollment runs Nov. 1 through Jan. 31, 2027, and people who want coverage starting Jan. 1 must pick a plan by Dec. 31. Twelve insurers offer plans, including one new insurer. About 725,000 enrollees pay $100 or less a month, including 358,000 who pay nothing, and 55% will see no increase in their monthly premium.

State subsidy funding rises from $190 million to $300 million, extending help to incomes up to 200% of the federal poverty level, or $31,920 for one person and $66,000 for a family of four. About 200,000 more people newly qualify, and nearly 200,000 can choose between two $0 Silver plans. The state money cannot fully replace roughly $2.5 billion a year in federal aid lost when enhanced federal credits expired. Free help is available at (800) 300-1506 or CoveredCA.com.
money: Shopping the 2027 plans, even if you like your current one, can reveal a lower premium or a $0 Silver option.
Check state-subsidy eligibility if your household income is near 200% of poverty.
Pick by Dec. 31 to avoid a coverage gap.
Free certified enrollers can find tax-credit eligibility you might miss.

Covered California kicks off 2027 open enrollment (Covered California)

stories.headline: Medi-Cal's Work Requirement Starts Jan. 1 for Adults 19-64, Followed by Six-Month Renewals Starting Mar. 1; Estimates Project Up to 2.1 Million Could Lose Coverage
stories.deck: Retroactive coverage shrinks to one month for adults without children, and some immigrant coverage ends June 30, 2027.
stories.summary: Work/volunteer/school hours from Jan. 1; six-month renewals Mar. 1; DHCS projects up to 1.8M disenrollments by June 2028.
paras: The state health department says Medi-Cal work, volunteer, school or training requirements begin Jan. 1, 2027 for adults 19-64 without children under 13, with exemptions. Retroactive coverage also shrinks that day, to one month for adults without children and two months for others. Starting March 1, 2027, some adults must renew every six months instead of annually, and missed deadlines can cost coverage.

One state-focused summary says the requirement is 80 hours a month or equivalent earnings and cites a DHCS projection of up to 1.8 million disenrollments by June 2028, versus about 2.1 million from the Legislative Analyst's Office, with some people shifting to Covered California or employer plans. Immigrant-related changes include federally funded coverage narrowing Oct. 1, 2026, and state-funded full-scope coverage ending June 30, 2027 for affected members. Copays of up to 5% of household income begin Oct. 1, 2028.
money: Keep your address, phone and email current with your county so you get renewal notices.
Ask your county early about exemptions and how to report hours.
If you lose Medi-Cal, check Covered California; losing coverage opens a special enrollment period in many cases.
Keep pay stubs and volunteer logs to prove hours.

sources.t: Tracking federal impact: Medi-Cal eligibility (DHCS)

stories.headline: CalFresh Work Rules: Adults 18-64 Without Young Children Must Average 20 Hours a Week to Keep Benefits Past Three Months, and Alpine County Lost Its Waiver Nov. 1
stories.deck: Seven counties are waived through Oct. 31, 2027: Colusa, Imperial, Kings, Merced, Monterey, Plumas and Tulare.
stories.summary: 3 months in 3 years without work, training or an exemption; groups newly covered include ages 55-64 and veterans.
paras: California's social services department says adults 18 to 64 who can work and do not live with a CalFresh member under 14 must work an average of 20 hours a week, volunteer, or be in school or training, or they can receive CalFresh for only three months in a three-year period. As of June 1, 2026, people 55 to 64, parents whose youngest child is 14 or older, people experiencing homelessness, veterans and former foster youth are newly subject to the rules unless another exemption applies.

County waivers for Nov. 1, 2026 through Oct. 31, 2027 cover Colusa, Imperial, Kings, Merced, Monterey, Plumas and Tulare; Alpine County's waiver ended Oct. 31. A local report said the work test can be met by earning at least $217.50 a week before taxes. Exemptions include disability, pregnancy and conditions that prevent 20 hours of work.
money: Use the state's pre-screening tool or call 1-877-847-3663 to see if you are exempt before losing benefits.
Report work, volunteer or school hours promptly; missing paperwork is a common reason for loss.
Food banks and school meal programs can fill gaps while you sort out eligibility.
Veterans and former foster youth should ask about exemptions.

sources.t: CalFresh able-bodied adults without dependents (California Department of Social Services)
New CalFresh work requirements start June 1 (KTVU)

stories.headline: MyFirstEV: Up to $3,500 Off a First Electric Vehicle, $1,750 Off a Used One, Applied at the Dealership With a $270 Million Fund
stories.deck: New cars must carry an MSRP of $50,000 or less and used cars must cost $25,000 or less.
stories.summary: Instant discount for first-time EV buyers; battery-electric only; participating automakers phase in through November.
paras: California's MyFirstEV program gives first-time zero-emission-vehicle buyers or lessees up to $3,500 off a new car and up to $1,750 off a used one, applied at the point of sale with no separate claim. New vehicles must have an MSRP up to $50,000, and used ones must cost up to $25,000 and be sold through a manufacturer's pre-owned program. Another report says the fund is $270 million, split between the state budget and automakers, and that hybrids do not qualify.

Hyundai, Lucid and Tesla were first; Ford, Rivian, Chevrolet and Kia were due in August, Toyota/Lexus, Honda and Subaru in September and Mitsubishi from November, with Nissan and Volvo undated. The sources did not mention income caps.
money: Ask the dealer to confirm the discount is applied before you sign; check that your brand is participating.
Gas still above $5.60 makes EV running costs attractive, but compare home-charging costs and your utility's EV rate plan.
Funds are finite; shoppers sometimes act sooner to avoid running out.
Used-EV eligibility is limited to manufacturer programs, so private-party sales do not qualify.

sources.t: California activates $3,500 rebates for first-time ZEV buyers (Electrive)
California's MyFirstEV provides a $3,500 instant rebate (Engadget)
